situation:
You and your teammate are the human resources director and the procurement director at MERIDIAN FRAME & DECK, a structural steel subcontractor that erects framing for commercial builders across three states. The chief operating officer (judge) oversees both of your departments and has asked to meet with the two of you this afternoon about a supplier question that has turned into a question about people.

Nine months ago MERIDIAN acquired CROSSCUT ERECTORS, a smaller competitor with its own crews, its own foremen, and its own way of buying material. The integration is not finished. Crosscut's field leaders still report through their old chain, still use suppliers Meridian never vetted, and still call themselves Crosscut people. Leadership here has not yet earned much credit with them.

One of the suppliers Meridian inherited is HANWEI FASTENING WORKS, an overseas manufacturer Crosscut has bought from for close to fifteen years. Two months ago Meridian paid for an independent labor audit of the Hanwei plant. The auditors visited twice, interviewed workers away from the factory, and rated the plant clean on wages, hours, and the age of its workforce. By that record the inherited supplier looks better than two mills Meridian already buys from.

Last week a Crosscut field superintendent who has walked that plant three times came to the human resources director privately and said the audit does not match what the visits showed: shifts running past anything on the posted schedule, and workers going quiet whenever the tour reached them. The superintendent asked that the source of the account stay confidential. No one else has corroborated it, and no other name at Crosscut carries as much weight with the foremen.

Hanwei fasteners are already specified on two hotel projects now in framing. Keeping the supplier means telling the superintendent that an audit outweighs what the superintendent saw, in the same season Crosscut's crews are deciding whether Meridian listens to them at all. Suspending the supplier means paying a domestic mill's higher price, pushing both hotel schedules back, and cutting off a fifteen-year partner on an account nothing else supports.

The chief operating officer (judge) wants your recommendation on whether Meridian keeps buying from Hanwei, wants to know how the decision will be carried back to the superintendent without breaking the confidence that was asked for, and wants a schedule for when and how the rest of the crews hear it. The chief operating officer (judge) will greet you, ask to hear your ideas, and will thank you after your presentation and questions.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the chief operating officer (judge) of MERIDIAN FRAME & DECK. Business background is the same as the situation above. You commissioned the labor audit of HANWEI FASTENING WORKS, you have read the clean result, and you have been told that a Crosscut field superintendent came forward privately with a very different account of the same plant and asked that the source stay confidential.

You want the human resources director and the procurement director to recommend whether Meridian keeps buying from Hanwei, to explain how that decision will be carried back to the superintendent without breaking the confidence, and to give you a schedule for when and how the rest of the crews hear it.

After the participant team has presented and has answered your questions, you will ask the following questions of each team:
judgeQuestions: How should we tell the superintendent what we decided?
